_about: Craft terms explained, each anchored in four Tamil films the Studio already teaches from. Definitions and examples are original analysis — no plot text or dialogue is reproduced from the films. `tanglish` mirrors the English gloss the way the blueprints already do. Terms are matched case-insensitively against step prose by autoTagGlossary() in src/ui/chrome.js; `aliases` catch the inflections that appear in the copy.

terms.def: One sentence carrying the protagonist, their want, the obstacle, and the cost of failure. If it needs a second sentence, the story is not yet decided.
terms.tanglish: Oru vaakkiyathula padam. Hero yaaru, enna venum, edhu thadukkudhu, thotta enna nashtam.

examples.note: A college dropout buys a fake degree to land a corporate job, and must clear 48 real arrears in three months when the one man who knows recognises him.
A fearful rookie officer must out-think a serial killer before his own nerve, not the case, defeats him.
Two people who loved each other at sixteen get one night, twenty-two years later, to say what they never said.
An encounter cop hunting a gangster is handed three stories that make his own certainty unusable.

terms.def: What is actually lost if the protagonist fails. Stakes must be specific and personal — 'the city is in danger' is a premise, not a stake.
terms.tanglish: Thotta enna poidum. Podhuvaa 'ooru azhiyum' illa — ivanukku personal-aa enna poidum.

examples.note: Exposure costs him the job, the engagement, and his father's belief — three separate losses, each with a face attached.
Nothing external is at risk at all. The stake is that the thing unsaid at sixteen stays unsaid forever. Proof that internal stakes carry a whole film.
The next victim is the public stake; the private one is whether the rookie stays a man who runs.
What is at risk is not the cop's life but his right to believe he is the good one.

terms.def: The argument the film makes, not the topic it covers. State it as a sentence someone could disagree with.
terms.tanglish: Padam enna vaadhaadudhu. Subject illa — oru statement, yaaraavadhu maruththu pesa mudiyanum.

examples.note: A shortcut is a debt, and it is collected with interest from people who did not take it.
Some loves are complete precisely because they were never consummated.
Courage is not the absence of fear but the decision to keep looking.
Good and evil are positions, and position depends on where you are standing.

terms.def: The conscious, stateable goal the protagonist would name if asked. It drives the plot. It is usually the wrong thing.
terms.tanglish: Avanukku theriyura aasai. Kepta sollum goal. Adhu porumbaaluma thappaana vishayam.

examples.note: A salary big enough to outrank his ex-girlfriend's fiancé. He can say it out loud, and it is entirely about being seen.
One more evening in the same room. Small, sayable, and not actually what he is missing.
To close the case — a want handed to him by rank rather than chosen.
To find and finish Vedha, cleanly, the way the previous encounters went.

terms.def: What the protagonist must accept to be whole, usually unknown to them and often the opposite of the want. The arc is the distance between the two.
terms.tanglish: Avanukku theriyaama theva-padra vishayam. Want-ukku ethir-maari irukkum. Arc-nu solradhu inda rendukkum edaila ulla dooram.

examples.note: Self-respect he did not fake. He gets it only after confessing and serving the sentence — the want (status) is destroyed to reach it.
To let the memory be enough. The want (more time) is refused, and the need is met anyway.
To stop outsourcing his nerve to the senior officer standing next to him.
To admit that his certainty was a convenience, not a moral position.

terms.def: The false belief about themselves or the world that the protagonist carries at page one. The story exists to test it.
terms.tanglish: Modhal page-la character nambura poi. Kadhai adha odaikkardhukku thaan irukku.

examples.note: 'The result is what counts; how I got it is nobody's business.' The film spends its whole second half billing him for that sentence.
'If I do not touch it, it stays perfect.' True and ruinous at the same time — the film never quite calls it a lie.
'I am not built for this work.' Held so firmly it nearly becomes true.
'I only shoot the guilty, so I am clean.'

terms.def: The event that makes the old normal unavailable. Not the first dramatic thing that happens — the first thing the protagonist cannot ignore.
terms.tanglish: Pazhaya normal-a thirumba mudiyaadha padi maathura event. Modhal drama illa — avanaala ignore panna mudiyaadha modhal vishayam.

examples.note: The dean recognises him. Everything before that is setup; from here the clock and the blackmail exist.
The reunion invitation. Trivial on paper, and it reopens twenty-two years.
The posting itself — the rookie is placed beside the one man who will not let him look away.
Vedha walks into the station and surrenders, choosing the terms of his own capture.

terms.def: The measurable change in what a character believes, shown through choices rather than stated. Write the first and last decision; the arc is the line between them.
terms.tanglish: Character-oda nambikkai maaradhu, dialogue-la sollaama choice-la kaatta-num. Modhal decision, kadaisi decision — adhukku naduvula thaan arc.

examples.note: First decision: buy the degree. Last decision: confess to four separate people with nothing left to gain. Same man, inverted.
Textbook positive arc — the trainee who flinches becomes the one who makes the deduction that closes the case.
A deliberate flat arc. Neither changes, and the film is about discovering they did not need to.
The cop's certainty erodes in three stages, one per story told to him.

terms.def: A detail placed early so a later payoff feels earned rather than convenient. A good setup has its own reason to be in the scene.
terms.tanglish: Munnadiye vechu, appuram use panna detail. Nalla setup-ku andha scene-la thaniyaa oru reason irukkum.

examples.note: The odd reverse-gear sound, dropped inside a confession about something else entirely. It is a character detail first and a clue second — which is why it does not announce itself.
The 48 arrears are a running joke long before they become the mechanism of the plot.
Photographs, established as his profession, become the film's method of holding time.
The folk-tale frame is stated up front, so the structure itself is the setup.

terms.def: The later moment a setup pays for. The audience should feel they could have seen it coming and did not.
terms.tanglish: Setup panna vishayam palan tharura edam. Paarthavanga 'ithu munnadiye irundhuchey' nu unara-num, aana andha nerathula theriyakoodaadhu.

examples.note: That reverse-gear sound identifies the vehicle and the killer. The clue was always audible; the film simply refused to point at it.
The arrears he treated as a joke become the exact measure of the debt he has to clear.
Each folk tale pays off as a moral trap the cop has already walked into.
The song withheld for most of the film finally arrives, and carries everything unspoken with it.

terms.def: The centre turn where the protagonist stops reacting and starts acting, usually on new information that reframes the problem.
terms.tanglish: Nadu-la varura thirupam. Ithu varaikkum react panninavan, ippo thaane move edukka aarambikaraan.

examples.note: He stops dodging the dean and commits to actually clearing the arrears — the goal shifts from hiding to doing.
The prime suspect turns out to be a teacher of the method, not its user. The case the team was solving no longer exists.
The second tale lands and the cop begins interrogating his own record instead of the gangster.
The reunion ends and the night becomes private. The film changes from group nostalgia to two people.

terms.def: Anything standing between the protagonist and the want. The best obstacles are people with their own defensible reasons.
terms.tanglish: Hero-kum avan aasaikkum naduvula nikkura edhuvum. Nalla obstacle-nu solradhu — sariyaana karanam vechirukkura oru manushan.

examples.note: The dean is not a villain. He is a man enforcing a rule that is entirely correct, which is what makes him immovable.
The obstacle is a marriage nobody in the film treats as an enemy, and the characters' own decency.
The rookie's own fear obstructs him more often than the killer does.
The obstacle is an argument, not a man — Vedha's questions, which cannot be shot.

terms.def: What the scene is about while the characters discuss something else. If the dialogue states the feeling, the subtext has been deleted.
terms.tanglish: Pesaradhu onnu, scene-oda artham innonnu. Feeling-a dialogue-la nerada sonna, subtext poidum.

examples.note: Almost the entire film. Two people discuss school, food, and a song, and never once state the thing the scene is about.
Each folk tale is a confession disguised as a riddle.
The banter with his friends keeps circling money and worth without either word being the subject.
The senior officer's instruction is always procedural on the surface and always about the junior's nerve underneath.

terms.def: Information the audience needs. The craft is not avoiding it but hiding it inside conflict, so it arrives while attention is elsewhere.
terms.tanglish: Paarvaiyaalarukku theriya vendiya thagaval. Thavirkuradhu illa — conflict-ukkulla olichu kudukkuradhu thaan vidhai.

examples.note: Procedure is explained to the trainee, so the audience learns the rules while a character is being tested on them.
Backstory is delivered as three tales the antagonist chooses to tell — exposition becomes an act of aggression.
The arrears count is repeated as comedy long before it has to be understood as arithmetic.
Twenty-two missing years are conveyed by what the two avoid asking.

terms.def: The moment the protagonist makes the choice the whole film has been arranging. It answers the theme, not just the plot.
terms.tanglish: Padam muzhusaa thayaar panna andha choice-a hero edukkura edam. Plot-ukku mattum illa, theme-ukkum badhil.

examples.note: The confession. He is not caught — he chooses the loss, which is the only move that answers the theme.
The rookie makes the deduction alone. The case closes because the arc completed, not the other way round.
The parting. Refusing the want is the climax.
The cop has to answer the last question himself, with no third story coming to save him.

terms.def: New information that reorganises everything already seen. A twist that only surprises is a trick; a reveal makes the earlier scenes mean more on a second watch.
terms.tanglish: Munnadi paartha ellathaiyum maathi amaikkura pudhu thagaval. Suma shock kudukkuradhu trick — nalla reveal, rendaam murai paakkumbodhu scene-ellam perusaa theriyum.

examples.note: The suspect is a killer, just not this one — he taught the method. Every interrogation scene before it changes meaning.
The classmate's ruined life lands as a reveal about the protagonist rather than the plot: the cost was always being paid by someone else.
Each tale reveals that the cop is already inside the story he is being told.
The film withholds almost nothing factually, and still reveals — what changes is what the audience understands the silence to mean.

terms.def: The character whose choices drive the story and whose belief is tested. Not necessarily the most screen time — the one who changes, or refuses to.
terms.tanglish: Yaaroda choice kadhaiya nagarthudho, yaaroda nambikkai test aagudho avan thaan. Screen time mukkiyam illa.

examples.note: Ragavan. Every plot turn is caused by a decision he made, including the ones that destroy him.
The trainee, not the senior officer — the film belongs to whoever is being changed by it.
Shared almost equally, which is rare and a deliberate structural risk.
The cop, even though the gangster has the better lines and controls the telling.

terms.def: The force opposing the want. Strongest when it is a person with a coherent philosophy rather than a person with bad intentions.
terms.tanglish: Hero-oda aasaiku ethiraana sakthi. Ketta ennam ulla aal illa — sariyaana logic vechirukkuravan thaan strong antagonist.

examples.note: The purest example here: the antagonist's position is arguable, and the film lets him argue it.
The dean opposes him with nothing but a correct rule, which is harder to fight than malice.
A killer with a private and coherent logic, which is exactly what makes him findable.
No antagonist at all — time is the opposition. Worth studying for how a film holds without one.

terms.def: The line that opens a scene: interior or exterior, where, and what time of day. It is not decoration — it is the unit the whole schedule is built from, because every department reads it to work out what a day costs.
terms.tanglish: Scene oda mudhal line — INT/EXT, edam, neram. Idhu vechu thaan schedule-um budget-um decide aagum.

examples.note: Time of day is doing the structural work: the same place at a different hour is a different scene with a different meaning, and the heading is where that turn is declared.
Interiors dominate, and the headings show it — a procedural gains pressure by refusing to go outside, and the slug list is where that choice becomes visible before a frame is shot.
A handful of locations recur under many headings. Repetition in the slug list is not poverty of invention; it is how a film makes a place feel inescapable.
Headings alternate between two worlds on a rhythm. Read the slug list alone and the film's structure is already legible.

terms.def: An edit that joins two shots by a shared shape, movement or sound, so the cut reads as a rhyme rather than a break. It makes a comparison the dialogue never has to state.
terms.tanglish: Rendu shot-ah ore maadhiri shape illa sound vechu join panradhu. Cut-e oru comparison aagidum, dialogue la sollave vendaam.

examples.note: Cuts across time rhyme on posture and framing, so two decades read as one continuous person rather than a flashback bolted on.
Sound carries across cuts more than image does; an edit joined on a noise keeps the dread continuous while the location changes.
Rhyming cuts are used for comedy first and consequence later — the same visual joke returns once it has stopped being funny.
The film rhymes its two protagonists by cutting on matched actions, arguing they are the same man before the script says so.

terms.def: The smallest unit of change. A scene is made of beats, and a beat ends when something turns — a decision, a refusal, a piece of information that cannot be taken back. A scene with no beat is a scene with no reason to exist.
terms.tanglish: Sinna maatram. Oru scene la edhachum thirumbina, adhu oru beat. Beat illana andha scene-ku velaye illa.

examples.note: Beats are small enough to be almost invisible — a question not answered, a glance held a moment too long — which is why the film can run on conversation alone.
Each beat hands the protagonist a piece of information that raises what he stands to lose, so the investigation and the character test advance on the same move.
Beats turn on arithmetic: every scene changes a number the protagonist is trying not to look at.
The beats are staged as questions put to the other man, so each turn advances the argument and the plot in the same line.

terms.def: The first spark of a film: a situation, a person or a question you cannot stop thinking about. It is not yet a story; it becomes one when you can say who wants what and what stands in the way.
terms.tanglish: Padam-oda modhal porigai. Oru situation, oru aal, illa oru kelvi. Yaar-ku enna venum, edhu thadukkudhu-nu sollum bodhu thaan adhu kadhai aagum.

examples.note: A young man talks his way into a corporate job on a forged degree and is recognised. One situation with a clock already inside it.
Two classmates, one reunion night, twenty-two years apart. The idea is a single evening with a question hanging over it.
A frightened rookie is paired with an unforgiving veteran on a murder case. The idea holds two problems at once: the crime and his nerve.
A cop hunts a gangster who answers only with stories. The idea is a hunt that turns into an argument.

terms.def: One working document that holds the decisions of your story: premise, characters, world, rules and arc. You read it before writing so every scene stays consistent with the rest.
terms.tanglish: Kadhai-oda ella mudivum oru idathula: premise, characters, ulagam, rules. Ezhudhum bodhu ithaye paarthu ezhudhanum.

examples.note: Its bible would pin down the forged degree, the count of unfinished papers and the dean's rule, because the plot is arithmetic that must never contradict itself.
A bible would fix who left when and what each person never said, so the reunion night stays consistent from the first line to the last.
It would hold the killer's fixed pattern, since the investigation only works if the method never changes between one scene and the next.
It would list the three stories and how each shifts the cop's certainty, because the structure is announced in advance and must hold.

terms.def: A short portrait of a person in your story: who they are, what they want, what they fear and what flaw holds them back. Enough to predict what they would do in a scene you have not written.
terms.tanglish: Oru character yaaru-nu sinnadhaa ezhudhi vaikkradhu: enna venum, edhukku bayam, enna kuraai. Ezhudhaadha scene-la avan enna pannuvaan-nu sollidanum.

examples.note: Ragavan is persuasive and believes results are the only thing anybody audits. That profile explains why he buys a shortcut.
Ram is restrained to the point of silence; Janaki is warm but will not pretend. Two profiles that make one quiet night tense.
Prakash is capable on paper and unsteady in the room; Loganathan is armoured by detachment. Opposite profiles on one case.
Vikram trusts a clean record as proof of a clean conscience. His profile is exactly what the film puts to the test.

terms.def: The characters around the protagonist who each press on one side of them: a mirror, an ally, an obstacle. Each should exist for a reason the story needs.
terms.tanglish: Hero-va sutthi irukkura characters. Ovvoruthar-um hero-oda oru pakkatha test pannanum, summa irukka koodaadhu.

examples.note: The classmate is a mirror who prices the protagonist's choice. They stay static on purpose, so the cost is easy to read.
Janaki is the mirror: she holds the other half of the question, so the protagonist cannot answer it alone.
Loganathan states the rules of the work aloud, so procedure becomes a continuous examination of the rookie.
Priya is the control group: she already holds the position the protagonist claims to hold, and the gap is the argument.

terms.def: The wrong belief or habit that keeps a character from what they need. The best flaws feel like strengths to the person who has them.
terms.tanglish: Character-ku thevaiyaanadhu kidaikkaama thadukkura thappaana nambikkai. Nalla flaw-a avan strength-nu nenaippaan.

examples.note: Ragavan believes the result is the only thing anybody audits, so he buys the outcome instead of earning it.
Ram mistakes restraint for integrity: he will not ask for anything he is not offered.
Prakash treats his fear as a verdict on what he is, rather than a condition he is in.
Vikram confuses a clean record with a clean conscience.

terms.def: What a character most dreads facing or losing. It drives their choices, usually in ways they would not admit out loud.
terms.tanglish: Character edhukku romba payapadraan. Adhu thaan avan mudivugalai odikkum, aana avan othukka maattaan.

examples.note: Ragavan wants status the people who wrote him off cannot ignore, which points to a fear of being written off again.
Ram never asks for what he wants unless it is offered, which points to a fear of asking and being refused.
Prakash fears his own nerve failing in the room, and the film never lets a later scene forgive the flinch.
Vikram fears finding out his certainty was a convenience rather than a moral position.

terms.def: A past hurt that shaped the character's flaw and their lie. It usually sits before page one and is revealed late, if at all.
terms.tanglish: Pazhaya kaayam, adhu thaan flaw-um poi-um uruvaakkudhu. Modhal page-ku munnaadiye irukkum, kadaisila thaan therium.

examples.note: Being written off is the wound that explains why the protagonist buys the outcome instead of earning it.
Twenty-two years of things unsaid are the wound the reunion presses on.
The film shows the habit, a flinch in the room, before it explains anything about where it came from.
The pressure here comes from outside: three stories erode his certainty in stages instead of one old injury.

terms.def: The struggle between what a character wants and what stands in their way: another person, the world, or themselves. Without it a scene has nothing to decide.
terms.tanglish: Avan aasaikkum, avanai thadukkuradhukkum naduvula nadakkura mothal. Idhu illaama scene-la mudivu edukka onnum irukkaadhu.

examples.note: The debt is real and the clock is short, and every day spent paying it is a day the invented life can collapse on its own.
Both have lived twenty-two years that cannot be undone, and neither will say so directly.
Every step of the procedure demands exactly the composure the rookie does not have.
The antagonist opposes him with an argument rather than force, and an argument cannot be shot.

terms.def: Where and when the story happens and the rules that hold there: its places, customs and limits. A clear world makes choices feel real.
terms.tanglish: Kadhai nadakkura idam, kaalam, adhula irukkura rules. Ulagam theliva irundha choice nijamaa theriyum.

examples.note: A college and a corporate job joined by one forged document. The dean enforces the rule that holds the whole world together.
A school reunion: a small, closed world in which one evening is the whole clock.
A police investigation whose procedure is stated aloud, so the rules of the world double as exposition.
An encounter cop's world where his method is routine and sanctioned, which the film then puts on trial.

terms.def: A list of the story's key turns in order, such as opening, inciting incident, midpoint and climax. It is a map of what changes, not a plan of every scene.
terms.tanglish: Kadhaila mukkiya thirupangal varisaiyaa. Ovvoru scene-um illa. Enna maarudhu-nu oru map.

examples.note: The opening plays as comedy with a fluent bluffer. The inciting beat is recognition, which starts the clock.
The beats are quiet: a reunion, the same room, the night narrowing to two people, facts stated, a short exchange as the climax.
The midpoint invalidates what the team thought it was solving, so the rookie starts producing theories of his own.
The first story declares the form, the second reverses the investigation, and the climax withholds the device the audience expects.

terms.def: A scene-by-scene list of the story in plain sentences, one line per scene, written before any dialogue. It shows whether the order of scenes works.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue ezhudhurathukku munnaadi, oru scene-ku oru vari-nu kadhaiya varisaiyaa ezhudhuradhu. Order work aagudha-nu theriyum.

examples.note: One line per scene, for example "he is recognised and the clock starts". Each line should name what changes.
"The two are in the same room and the question changes." Quiet films need the change named most clearly.
"The case stops being what the team thought; he starts producing theories." One line per turn keeps an investigation readable.
"The second story lands and the search turns on the cop's own record." The outline shows the structure before dialogue exists.

terms.def: A short prose summary of the whole story from beginning to end, including the ending. Producers and festivals read it, and it proves the story is decided.
terms.tanglish: Kadhai muzhusaiyum, mudivu sethu, sinnadhaa ezhudhuradhu. Padikkaravanga kadhai mudivaachu-nu nambanum.

examples.note: A forged degree, a recognition, a term to clear the papers, and a choice at the end of the lie. The synopsis ends on the choice, not on a twist.
Brief on plot and honest about it: a reunion, one night, a quiet exchange, and lives that resume.
A rookie, a veteran and a methodical killer. The synopsis should say the case closes as a result of his arc completing.
An encounter cop, a gangster who tells stories, and a final question the cop has to answer for himself.

terms.def: The film written as pages: scene headings, action, character names and dialogue in a fixed format the whole crew can read. One page is roughly one minute of screen time.
terms.tanglish: Padam-a page-aa ezhudhuradhu: scene heading, action, dialogue, oru standard format-la. Oru page, oru nimidam.

examples.note: Both its comic opening and its later arithmetic have to be shown on the page: what the camera sees and what is said.
Mostly dialogue and staging: distance, who looks away first, shown through action lines.
Procedure on the page: the veteran states the rules aloud, so action and dialogue both carry the lesson.
Stories told in dialogue become scenes of their own, and the page has to give the telling to the person who profits from it.

terms.def: Everything the audience sees and hears that is not dialogue, written in the present tense. Describe only what a camera or microphone can capture.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue illaadha ellam: kaamera-la theriyaradhu, ketkuradhu. Ippo nadakkura maadhiri present tense-la ezhudhunga.

examples.note: A character performing a fluency he does not have is written as what we see him do, not as what he feels.
Distance, glances and who looks away first are action lines: the staging carries what the dialogue avoids.
The rookie's physical reaction to the work is an action line: visible, unglamorous, and never explained.
A look across a table between the cop and the gangster is action. The page shows it and does not explain it.

terms.def: The character's name in capitals above their dialogue, so the reader and the actor know who is speaking. Spell it the same way every time.
terms.tanglish: Dialogue-ku mela capital-la character peyar. Yaaru pesaraanga-nu theriya. Ovvoru thadavaiyum ore maadhiri ezhudhunga.

examples.note: RAGAVAN above his lines. The cast list and breakdown match speakers by that exact name.
RAM and JANAKI, spelled the same every time, so the cast list counts two people and not four.
PRAKASH and LOGANATHAN: the cue is the name the cast list will use, so keep it identical page to page.
VIKRAM and VEDHA: two cues in an argument. Consistent names keep the screen-time count right.

terms.def: What characters say out loud. Good dialogue sounds like speech, carries what the character wants, and often leaves the real feeling unsaid.
terms.tanglish: Character-gal pesaradhu. Nijam pesara maadhiri irukkanum, aasaiya kaatanum, unmaiyaana feeling-a sollaama vidanum.

examples.note: Early dialogue is bluff and charm: the persuasion that later indicts the protagonist.
The dialogue stays on logistics and old classmates while the staging carries the real content.
The veteran states the rules of the work aloud, so dialogue doubles as exposition and as an examination of the rookie.
Told as stories: each is a deliberate choice by the speaker, which makes dialogue an act of aggression.

terms.def: A short direction in brackets under a character name, such as (quietly) or (to the door). Use it only when the line could be read two ways.
terms.tanglish: Character peyar-ku keezha bracket-la sinna direction: (mella) maadhiri. Line-ku rendu artham varumbodhu mattum use pannunga.

examples.note: A confident pitch could be sincere or a bluff. A parenthetical settles it only where the scene does not already.
Where a plain line hides feeling, resist (sadly): let staging carry it and keep brackets for real ambiguity.
Under pressure the rookie's line might need (steadily) against a shaking read: one word of direction, not a paragraph.
When the gangster answers a question with a question, a parenthetical is rarely needed. The structure tells the actor.

terms.def: An instruction between scenes such as CUT TO: or FADE OUT. Modern scripts use few, because a clean scene heading already implies a cut.
terms.tanglish: Rendu scene-ku naduvula CUT TO: maadhiri line. Ippo romba use panna maattaanga, scene heading-e cut-nu artham.

examples.note: Most cuts between its scenes need no marking. A deliberate echo from an early joke to a later number might.
A slow evening moves from scene to scene on plain headings. A transition would add nothing.
The investigation moves by headings. Keep a marked transition for a real jump, such as a gap in time.
A cut from one story back to the interrogation is a real change, one of the few places a marked transition could earn its line.

terms.def: CONT'D beside a character name means the same person is speaking again after an action line. It tells the reader it is one speech, not a new one.
terms.tanglish: Oru character pesi, naduvula action vandhu, thirumbi avane pesinaa CONT'D. Adhu oru speech-ae.

examples.note: Ragavan's pitch is broken by a glance across the room, then resumes: his cue gets (CONT'D).
An action line sits between two lines from one person in a quiet exchange: (CONT'D) shows it is one thought.
Loganathan lists a rule, an action line breaks in, and he continues: his cue gets (CONT'D).
Vedha begins a story, a beat of action interrupts, and the telling resumes under VEDHA (CONT'D).

terms.def: Reading the script scene by scene and listing everything each scene needs: cast, props, locations, vehicles, costumes. It is the first step in planning a shoot.
terms.tanglish: Script-a scene scene-aa padichu enna enna thevai-nu list pannuradhu: cast, props, location. Shoot plan-oda modhal step.

examples.note: A breakdown separates the scenes needing a campus from the ones needing an office, and lists who is needed in each.
A story built on one evening likely has a short list of places, so the weight of its breakdown sits on cast and props.
A procedural lists recurring roles and evidence props scene by scene, which makes the working set visible.
Interrogation scenes repeat a setting, and the breakdown groups them so the shoot can combine them.

terms.def: A schedule board with one strip per scene, ordered into shoot days by location, cast and time of day. It plans the shoot, not the story order.
terms.tanglish: Oru scene-ku oru strip. Location, cast, neram paathu shoot naal-kku varisai pannuvaanga. Kadhai order illa, shoot order.

examples.note: Scenes in the same place can be grouped into one day, even when the story visits them at different times.
Scenes in one place can be shot together, in whatever order suits the cast and the light.
Scenes with both the veteran and the rookie share cast, so a stripboard can cluster them into the days both are booked.
Scenes with both leads in the same room can be clustered into the days both actors are available.

terms.def: A chart showing which days each cast member or element is needed on the shoot. It shows who is booked when and where days can be saved.
terms.tanglish: Evvalavu naal yaar-yaar thevai-nu chart. Yaar eppo booking, enga naal micham pannalam-nu theriyum.

examples.note: The protagonist works almost every day, while the dean likely needs only a few. The chart makes that visible.
Two leads carry the film, so two rows are busiest and everyone else has short blocks.
The two leads are needed on most days, and the supporting roles show as short blocks.
Three principal roles overlap in different ways, and the chart shows how that sets the booking.

terms.def: The one-page plan for a single shoot day: scenes, cast and crew call times, location, weather and notes. The assistant director issues it the day before.
terms.tanglish: Oru shoot naal-ku oru page: scene, yaaru eppo varanum, location, notes. AD munnaadi naal anuppuvaar.

examples.note: A day set in the college lists the dean's call and the lead's together, since the scene needs both of them.
A night scene lists a late call, because call times follow when the scene and the light need people.
A procedural day lists both leads' calls and the props the scene needs, so nobody waits.
An interrogation day lists both leads and the location, with times set by when the room is free.

terms.def: A list of every camera set-up for each scene: the framing, the lens, the movement. The director and cinematographer write it from the script.
terms.tanglish: Ovvoru scene-ku camera set-up list: framing, lens, movement. Director-um cinematographer-um script-la irundhu seiyyuvaanga.

examples.note: A gag meant to become arithmetic later needs a clear close shot the first time, so the audience memorises it for fun.
Where staging carries the feeling, the list needs the wide that shows the distance and the close that shows who looks away.
The rookie's physical reaction needs a close shot before the film moves on.
A face-to-face argument is planned as shot and reverse shot, and the list says which speaker each set-up favours.
